claim: Sexual reproduction can either facilitate or restrain transposable element (TE) accumulation by providing TEs with a means of spreading to all individuals in a population, versus facilitating TE load reduction via purifying selection.
source: Theory predicts that sexual reproduction can either facilitate or restrain transposable element (TE) accumulation by providing TEs with a means of spreading to all individuals in a population, versus facilitating TE load reduction via purifying selection.
evidence: This claim is supported by theoretical predictions referenced in the abstract and introduction.

claim: TE loads decrease rapidly under asexual reproduction in experimental Saccharomyces cerevisiae populations.
source: By quantifying genomic TE loads over time in experimental sexual and asexual Saccharomyces cerevisiae populations, we provide direct evidence that TE loads decrease rapidly under asexual reproduction.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study quantifying TE loads over time.

claim: The reduction in TE loads under asexual reproduction may occur via evolution of TE activity, most likely via increased excision rates.
source: We show, using simulations, that this reduction may occur via evolution of TE activity, most likely via increased excision rates.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results presented in the study.

claim: Sex is a major driver of genomic TE loads and at the root of the success of TEs.
source: Thus, sex is a major driver of genomic TE loads and at the root of the success of TEs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental and simulation results showing TE maintenance in sexual populations.

claim: Self-replicating transposable elements (TEs) can occupy large fractions of genomes in organisms throughout the tree of life.
source: Self-replicating transposable elements (TEs) can occupy large fractions of genomes in organisms throughout the tree of life (reviewed in Hua-Van et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: TEs proliferate independently of the host cell cycle via different self-copying mechanisms involving 'cut-and-paste' or 'copy-and-paste' systems.
source: Their overwhelming success is driven by their ability to proliferate independently of the host cell cycle via different self-copying mechanisms involving 'cut-and-paste' or 'copy-and-paste' systems.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about TE mechanisms.

claim: TEs can invade genomes in a similar way to parasites, despite generally not providing any advantage to the individual carrying them.
source: These mechanisms allow TEs to invade genomes in a similar way to parasites, despite generally not providing any advantage to the individual carrying them (Doolittle and Sapienza, 1980; Orgel and Crick, 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational papers on TE biology.

claim: TEs generate deleterious effects in their hosts by promoting ectopic recombination and because most new TE insertions in coding or regulatory sequences disrupt gene functions.
source: To the contrary, TEs generate deleterious effects in their hosts by promoting ectopic recombination and because most new TE insertions in coding or regulatory sequences disrupt gene functions (Finnegan, 1992; Montgomery et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on TE effects.

claim: Sexual reproduction can facilitate the accumulation of TEs because it allows TEs to colonise new genomes and spread throughout populations.
source: Sexual reproduction can facilitate the accumulation of TEs because it allows TEs to colonise new genomes and spread throughout populations (Hickey, 1982; Zeyl et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical and empirical studies.

claim: Sexual reproduction should favour the evolution of highly active TEs because the colonisation of new genomes is more likely for active TEs.
source: Because the colonisation of new genomes is more likely for active TEs, sexual reproduction should favour the evolution of highly active TEs (Charlesworth and Langley, 1986; Hickey, 1982), even though increased activity generates higher TE loads in the host genome.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical studies.

claim: Sexual reproduction facilitates the evolution of host defences and increases the efficacy of purifying selection against deleterious TE copies by reducing selective interference among loci.
source: At the same time, sexual reproduction facilitates the evolution of host defences and increases the efficacy of purifying selection against deleterious TE copies by reducing selective interference among loci (Ågren and Wright, 2011; Arkhipova and Meselson, 2005; Crespi and Schwander, 2012; Wright and Finnegan, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on the effects of sexual reproduction on selection.

claim: In the absence of sex, reduced purifying selection can result in the accumulation of TEs, unless TE copies get eliminated via excision at sufficiently high rates.
source: In the absence of sex, reduced purifying selection can thus result in the accumulation of TEs, unless TE copies get eliminated via excision at sufficiently high rates (Burt and Trivers, 2006; Dolgin and Charlesworth, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical studies.

claim: No consistent difference in genomic TE loads emerges between natural populations of asexual and related sexual organisms.
source: Genomic TE loads have been empirically estimated for natural populations of asexual and related sexual organisms, but no consistent difference emerges (Ågren et al., 2015; Bast et al., 2016; Jiang et al., 2017; Szitenberg et al., 2016), probably because many confounding factors not related to reproductive mode such as hybridisation and polyploidisation can affect TE loads and mask the effect of sex (Arkhipova and Rodriguez, 2013; Hua-Van et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies on TE loads in natural populations.

claim: Many confounding factors not related to reproductive mode such as hybridisation and polyploidisation can affect TE loads and mask the effect of sex.
source: Genomic TE loads have been empirically estimated for natural populations of asexual and related sexual organisms, but no consistent difference emerges (Ågren et al., 2015; Bast et al., 2016; Jiang et al., 2017; Szitenberg et al., 2016), probably because many confounding factors not related to reproductive mode such as hybridisation and polyploidisation can affect TE loads and mask the effect of sex (Arkhipova and Rodriguez, 2013; Hua-Van et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies discussing confounding factors in TE load studies.

claim: McDonald et al. maintained four sexual and four asexual strains originating from the same haploid ancestral strain (W303) under constant conditions over 1000 generations.
source: McDonald et al. maintained four sexual and four asexual strains originating from the same haploid ancestral strain (W303) under constant conditions over 1000 generations.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design from a previous study.

claim: For sexual strains, a mating event (meiosis) was induced every 90 generations.
source: For sexual strains, a mating event (meiosis) was induced every 90 generations.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design from a previous study.

claim: Sequencing of each strain was conducted at generation 0 and every 90 generations prior to mating.
source: Sequencing of each strain was conducted at generation 0 and every 90 generations prior to mating (for details see Materials and methods, and McDonald et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design from a previous study.

claim: TEs in S. cerevisiae are well characterised.
source: TEs in S. cerevisiae are well characterised (Carr et al., 2012; Castanera et al., 2016; Voytas and Boeke, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies characterizing S. cerevisiae TEs.

claim: S. cerevisiae TEs consist solely of 'copy-and-paste' elements that are flanked by long terminal repeats (LTRs) and are grouped into the families Ty1-Ty5.
source: S. cerevisiae TEs consist solely of 'copy-and-paste' elements that are flanked by long terminal repeats (LTRs) and are grouped into the families Ty1-Ty5 (Voytas and Boeke, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on S. cerevisiae TEs.

claim: The 12.2 Mb genome of the studied yeast strain comprises approximately 50 full-length, active Ty element copies, and 430 inactive ones.
source: The 12.2 Mb genome of the studied yeast strain comprises approximately 50 full-length, active Ty element copies, and 430 inactive ones (Carr et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study characterizing the yeast genome.

claim: Inactive TE copies include truncated elements as well as remnants from TE excisions (i.e., solo-LTR formation).
source: Inactive copies include truncated elements as well as remnants from TE excisions (i.e., solo-LTR formation; Carr et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study characterizing the yeast genome.

claim: Excisions occur by intra-chromosomal recombination between the two flanking LTRs of a TE, and result in the removal of protein-coding genes that allow for transposition.
source: Excisions occur by intra-chromosomal recombination between the two flanking LTRs of a TE, and result in the removal of protein-coding genes that allow for transposition.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about TE excision mechanisms.

claim: The total TE load in sexual strains remained constant over 1000 generations.
source: This analysis revealed that the total TE load in sexual strains remained constant over 1000 generations, but decreased in asexual strains over time (resulting in a total reduction of 23.5% after 1000 generations; generation effect p<0.001, reproductive mode effect p=0.081, and interaction between generation and mode p<0.001; permutation ANOVA, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The total TE load decreased in asexual strains over time, resulting in a total reduction of 23.5% after 1000 generations.
source: This analysis revealed that the total TE load in sexual strains remained constant over 1000 generations, but decreased in asexual strains over time (resulting in a total reduction of 23.5% after 1000 generations; generation effect p<0.001, reproductive mode effect p=0.081, and interaction between generation and mode p<0.001; permutation ANOVA, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The available sequencing data allowed detection of 24 out of the 50 full-length insertions that are present in the reference genome of the ancestral strain at the start of the experiment.
source: With a pipeline that combines different complementary approaches (Nelson et al., 2017, see Materials and methods), the available sequencing data allowed us to detect 24 out of the 50 full-length insertions that are present in the reference genome of the ancestral strain at the start of the experiment (generation 0).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data analysis methods and results.

claim: The number of (detectable) full-length TE copies remained constant in sexual yeast strains.
source: As with the first approach, we found that the number of (detectable) full-length TE copies remained constant in sexual yeast strains, but decreased in asexual strains over time (generation effect p=0.006, reproductive mode effect p=0.033, and interaction between generation and mode p<0.001; permutation ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: The number of (detectable) full-length TE copies decreased in asexual strains over time.
source: As with the first approach, we found that the number of (detectable) full-length TE copies remained constant in sexual yeast strains, but decreased in asexual strains over time (generation effect p=0.006, reproductive mode effect p=0.033, and interaction between generation and mode p<0.001; permutation ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: In asexual strains, the estimated average number of full-length TEs decreased from approximately 50 to 41 over 1000 generations.
source: In asexual strains, the estimated average number of full-length TEs decreased from approximately 50 to 41 over 1000 generations (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: 'Ancestral' TE insertions are lost at a higher rate in asexual than sexual strains.
source: These analyses revealed that 'ancestral' TE insertions are lost at a higher rate in asexual than sexual strains (generation effect p=0.002, reproductive mode effect p=0.027, and interaction between generation and mode p<0.001; permutation ANOVA), while we detected similar numbers of novel TE insertions (indicating similar transposition rates) under both reproductive modes (generation effect p=0.338, reproductive mode effect p=0.271, and interaction between generation and mode p=0.599; permutation ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Similar numbers of novel TE insertions were detected under both reproductive modes, indicating similar transposition rates.
source: These analyses revealed that 'ancestral' TE insertions are lost at a higher rate in asexual than sexual strains (generation effect p=0.002, reproductive mode effect p=0.027, and interaction between generation and mode p<0.001; permutation ANOVA), while we detected similar numbers of novel TE insertions (indicating similar transposition rates) under both reproductive modes (generation effect p=0.338, reproductive mode effect p=0.271, and interaction between generation and mode p=0.599; permutation ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Even very rare events of sex (just 10 out of 990 reproduction events) are sufficient to maintain genomic TE loads.
source: Taken together, our empirical observations indicate that even very rare events of sex (here just 10 out of 990 reproduction events) are sufficient to maintain genomic TE loads, while asexuality results in the reduction of TE loads.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing TE maintenance in sexual strains.

claim: Asexuality results in the reduction of TE loads.
source: Taken together, our empirical observations indicate that even very rare events of sex (here just 10 out of 990 reproduction events) are sufficient to maintain genomic TE loads, while asexuality results in the reduction of TE loads.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing TE reduction in asexual strains.

claim: The parallel reduction of TE loads in different asexual strains suggests that the evolution of reduced TE activity in asexual strains influences genomic TE loads more strongly than purifying selection.
source: The parallel reduction of TE loads in different asexual strains suggests that the evolution of reduced TE activity (the ratio of transposition to excision) in asexual strains influences genomic TE loads more strongly than purifying selection, which should act to reduce TE loads most effectively in sexual strains.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the parallel reduction observed across multiple asexual strains.

claim: For all simulations without modifier alleles, TE loads in populations undergoing sex every 90 generations decreased faster than in asexual populations.
source: For all simulations, TE loads in populations undergoing sex every 90 generations decreased faster than in asexual populations, contrary to our empirical observations.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results.

claim: Sexual events generate variation among individuals in TE loads (and thus variation in fitness), which facilitates selection against deleterious TEs.
source: This occurs because sexual events generate variation among individuals in TE loads (and thus variation in fitness), which facilitates selection against deleterious TEs (see also Dolgin and Charlesworth, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results and a citation to a theoretical study.

claim: Increased TE activity during meiosis only transiently increases TE loads in sexual strains.
source: Indeed, increased TE activity during meiosis only transiently increases TE loads in sexual strains.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results.

claim: Additional TE copies generated during meiosis are rapidly removed by purifying selection because increased TE activity generates increased variation in TE loads (and therefore in fitness) among strains.
source: Because such activity also generates increased variation in TE loads (and therefore in fitness) among strains, the additional TE copies generated during meiosis are rapidly removed by purifying selection (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: None of the simulations without modifier alleles generated the empirically observed pattern of lower TE loads in asexual than sexual strains.
source: In short, none of the simulations generated the empirically observed pattern of lower TE loads in asexual than sexual strains.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results.

claim: The modifier allele spreads rapidly to fixation in asexual strains because it is associated with genomes that have fewer TE copies, and therefore have a higher relative fitness.
source: In simulations that included the modifier allele, the modifier spreads rapidly to fixation in asexual strains, because it is associated with genomes that have fewer TE copies, and therefore have a higher relative fitness.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results.

claim: TE activity rates decrease in asexual populations when the modifier allele spreads to fixation.
source: As a consequence, TE activity rates decrease in asexual populations (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The modifier cannot spread as rapidly in sexual populations because recombination constantly breaks up the association between the modifier and less TE loaded backgrounds.
source: By contrast, the modifier cannot spread as rapidly in sexual populations because recombination constantly breaks up the association between the modifier and less TE loaded backgrounds.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results and theoretical reasoning.

claim: Parameter values representative for yeast result in simulations with a very close fit to the empirical results when allowing for the evolution of TE activity rates.
source: By allowing for the evolution of TE activity rates in our simulations, we were able to identify parameter values representative for yeast that result in simulations with a very close fit to our empirical results (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A likely mechanism driving genomic TE load reduction in asexual yeast strains is the rapid evolution of increased TE excision rates.
source: These analyses thus corroborate our empirical findings that a likely mechanism driving genomic TE load reduction in asexual yeast strains is the rapid evolution of increased TE excision rates.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results and empirical data.

claim: A similar effect would be expected if the modifier acted on transposition rather than excision rates, since the net TE activity depends on the relative rates of transposition vs excision.
source: A similar effect would be expected if our modifier acted on transposition rather than excision rates, since the net TE activity depends on the relative rates of transposition vs excision.
evidence: This claim is based on theoretical reasoning about TE dynamics.

claim: The empirical results do not suggest major differences in transposition rates between sexual and asexual yeast strains.
source: However, our empirical results do not suggest major differences in transposition rates between sexual and asexual yeast strains.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing similar numbers of novel TE insertions.

claim: In the absence of TE activity evolution, sexual strains always lose TEs faster than asexual ones.
source: In combination with our findings that, in the absence of TE activity evolution, sexual strains always lose TEs faster than asexual ones, the empirical results are best explained by an increase in TE excision rates under asexuality (Figures 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results.

claim: The empirical results are best explained by an increase in TE excision rates under asexuality.
source: In combination with our findings that, in the absence of TE activity evolution, sexual strains always lose TEs faster than asexual ones, the empirical results are best explained by an increase in TE excision rates under asexuality (Figures 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combination of simulation and empirical results.

claim: Sexual reproduction permits the maintenance of TEs in S. cerevisiae.
source: Our study shows that sexual reproduction permits the maintenance of TEs in S. cerevisiae, while in its absence, TE loads decrease, likely via the evolution of TE activity rates.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing TE maintenance in sexual strains.

claim: In the absence of sexual reproduction, TE loads decrease, likely via the evolution of TE activity rates.
source: Our study shows that sexual reproduction permits the maintenance of TEs in S. cerevisiae, while in its absence, TE loads decrease, likely via the evolution of TE activity rates.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and simulation results.

claim: The findings are consistent with empirical findings of low TE activity in old asexuals.
source: The findings are consistent with empirical findings of low TE activity in old asexuals (Bast et al., 2016) and the idea that TEs should evolve to be benign in asexual species, because the evolutionary interests of TEs and their host genome are aligned (Charlesworth and Langley, 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an empirical study.

claim: TEs should evolve to be benign in asexual species, because the evolutionary interests of TEs and their host genome are aligned.
source: The findings are consistent with empirical findings of low TE activity in old asexuals (Bast et al., 2016) and the idea that TEs should evolve to be benign in asexual species, because the evolutionary interests of TEs and their host genome are aligned (Charlesworth and Langley, 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a theoretical study.

claim: The simulations suggest that there is some form of TE defense mechanism (a 'modifier locus') that either segregates in the ancestral yeast strain used in the experiments or repeatedly appeared de novo during experimental evolution.
source: While the exact mechanisms causing TE activity change in the asexual yeast populations cannot be assessed in the empirical data, our simulations suggest that there is some form of TE defense mechanism (a 'modifier locus') that either segregates in the ancestral yeast strain used in the experiments or repeatedly appeared de novo during experimental evolution.
evidence: This claim is based on simulation results and speculation about the mechanism.

claim: TE loads do not increase, but decrease, in asexual populations.
source: Independently of the exact mechanism, we confirm that TE loads do not increase, but decrease, in asexual populations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The finding that TE loads decrease in asexual populations contrasts with the hypothesis that most asexual species are evolutionarily short lived because they are driven to extinction via negative consequences of accumulating TE copies.
source: This contrasts with the hypothesis that most asexual species are evolutionarily short lived because they are driven to extinction via negative consequences of accumulating TE copies (Arkhipova and Meselson, 2005).
evidence: This claim contrasts the study's findings with a hypothesis from a cited study.

claim: Sex is at the root of the evolutionary success of parasitic TEs.
source: Instead, sex is at the root of the evolutionary success of parasitic TEs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental and simulation results.

claim: Six haploid strains consisting of mating type a (MATa) and six haploid strains of mating type α (MATα) were grown over 990 generations.
source: For the experiment, six haploid strains consisting of mating type a (MATa) and six haploid strains of mating type α (MATα), were grown over 990 generations.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design.

claim: Four strains were grown exclusively asexually (two of MATa, two of MATα).
source: Of these, four strains were grown exclusively asexually (two of MATa, two of MATα), while the eight others (four of MATa, four of MATα) were mixed for mating events every 90 generations, resulting in four sexual strains.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design.

claim: Eight strains (four of MATa, four of MATα) were mixed for mating events every 90 generations, resulting in four sexual strains.
source: Of these, four strains were grown exclusively asexually (two of MATa, two of MATα), while the eight others (four of MATa, four of MATα) were mixed for mating events every 90 generations, resulting in four sexual strains.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design.

claim: Paired-end Illumina reads were generated for each of the 12 different strains every 90 generations during 990 generations (for a total of 11 sequencing events per strain).
source: Paired-end Illumina reads were generated for each of the 12 different strains every 90 generations during 990 generations (for a total of 11 sequencing events per strain).
evidence: This claim describes the sequencing methodology.

claim: Read numbers per sample ranged from 12,775 to 10,270,312, averaging 2,964,869 reads per sample, with a total of 818,303,966 reads.
source: Read numbers per sample ranged from 12,775 to 10,270,312, averaging 2,964,869 reads per sample, with a total of 818,303,966 reads.
evidence: This claim describes the sequencing data characteristics.

claim: Coverage influences the ability to detect TE insertions.
source: (A) TE insertions (including those present in the reference genome and de novo insertions) vs. median sequencing coverage from paired reads. Coverage influences the ability to detect TE insertions (Wilcoxon signed-rank test V = 4095, p-value<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Data from asexual strains had lower coverage than sexual strains.
source: (B) Median read coverage per sample for sexual (red) and asexual (blue) strains over 1000 generations. Data from asexual strains had lower coverage, but were not different to sexuals through time (generation effect p=0.096, reproductive mode effect p=0.002, and interaction between generation and mode p=0.588; permutation ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Asexual and sexual strains were not different in coverage through time.
source: (B) Median read coverage per sample for sexual (red) and asexual (blue) strains over 1000 generations. Data from asexual strains had lower coverage, but were not different to sexuals through time (generation effect p=0.096, reproductive mode effect p=0.002, and interaction between generation and mode p=0.588; permutation ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Subsampling to the mean asexual read coverage per generation for all samples results in similar findings.
source: (C) Subsampling to the mean asexual read coverage per generation for all samples results in similar findings (generation effect p=0.012, reproductive mode effect p=0.302, and interaction between generation and mode p=0.004; permutation ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Meiosis generates TE load spikes following events of sexual reproduction.
source: Meiosis generates the TE load spikes following events of sexual reproduction, but allows for selection to effectively remove genotypes with high TE loads by generating fitness variation among genotypes.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Meiosis allows for selection to effectively remove genotypes with high TE loads by generating fitness variation among genotypes.
source: Meiosis generates the TE load spikes following events of sexual reproduction, but allows for selection to effectively remove genotypes with high TE loads by generating fitness variation among genotypes.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Both empirical and simulation data show that asexuals lost about nine active, full-length TEs by generation 1000.
source: For both (A) empirical and (B) simulation data, asexuals lost about nine active, full-length TEs by generation 1000.
evidence: This claim is supported by both empirical data and simulation results shown in Figure 1.
